food.text: Central Asian cuisine was shaped by many cultures, and Turkic influence is seen in manti dumplings, a wheat porridge called sumalak and assorted dairy products. These foods show how nomadic and settled traditions in the region blended over time.
The Mongol invasions of the 13th century disrupted the region, yet Iranian and Turkic culinary traditions carried on. They lived on in Ottoman palace cuisine and survived into the 20th century.

Finno-Ugric peoples in Western Siberia were introduced to a filled dumpling by Iranian merchants during the Middle Ages. They named it pelnan, meaning "ear bread". The dish was adopted in Russia in the 17th century, where it is called pelmeni.

Mahmud al-Kashgari described several Central Asian cooking methods, including pit cooking, baking in earthenware and grilling. His account is one of the ways historians know how food was prepared in the Turkic world.

A dumpling called shishbarak is mentioned in Egyptian cookbooks of the 13th and 15th centuries. According to historian Daniel Newman, it was possibly imported into Egypt by Turkic tribes from the Central Asian Steppes.

art.text: During Timur's reign in the 14th century, the nomadic steppe culture of Central Asia fused with the settled culture of Iran. One result was an entirely new visual language that glorified Timur and the Timurid rulers who followed him. It was also used to express their commitment to Islam.

The Timurid Empire, founded by Timur in 1370, had a syncretic culture that combined Turkic, Mongolic, and Persian influences. It led to the Timurid Renaissance, particularly during the reign of Shahrukh Mirza and that of his son Ulugh Begh.

Large quantities of panni tartarici, or Tatar cloth, were recorded in the Papal inventory of 1295. They must have been diplomatic gifts from the Il-Khanate, whose rulers exchanged people and presents with Western powers between 1265 and 1308.

art.text: Around 1326, Ozbeg reopened friendly relations with the Yuan, recognising the economic benefits and the Genghisid legacy. He also strengthened ties with the Muslim world, building mosques and other elaborate structures such as baths.

Western merchants could buy Tatar cloth from Tabriz and from Sultaniya, the Mongol capital established by Öljaitü between 1305 and 1313. This trade lasted until the Mamluks captured the Cilician Armenia harbour of Ayas in 1347.

art.text: Mongols seen in European paintings of the late 13th and 14th centuries come from the diverse population of the Golden Horde, including Tatars, Finns, Slavs and people from the Caucasus. This suggests that Italian artists had been in direct contact with people from Tartary.

war.text: Steppe nomads' relations with settled peoples were marked by conflict, and their way of life suited warfare. Their horse archers, with devastating techniques, made them some of the most militarily potent people in the world. Because nomads made little that settled people wanted, raiding was the popular alternative to trade, and the steppe peoples forced scattered city states and kingdoms to pay tribute or face annihilation. Periodically, leaders would unite several tribes into one force that launched campaigns of conquest.

The gunpowder revolution allowed settled peoples to defeat steppe horsemen in open battle for the first time. Such weapons needed the infrastructure and economies of large societies, so nomads could not easily produce them. From the 15th century, settled powers gradually began to conquer Central Asia.

The Mongol Empire, which began its conquests under Genghis Khan in 1206 to 1207, conquered most of continental Asia and parts of Eastern Europe. It became the largest contiguous land empire in human history. Mounted archers were a major part of its armies.

In 1241 the Mongols attacked Central Europe with three separate armies. Two went through Poland, winning several victories and defeating the army of Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia at Legnica. The main army under Batu Khan and Subutai entered Hungary through the fortified Verecke Pass and annihilated the army of the count palatine Denis Tomaj on 12 March 1241. Batu's brother Shiban marched in an arc north of the main force.

At Kalka River in 1223, the Mongols under Jebe and Subutai defeated a Rus' coalition using the ancient horse-archer tactic of the feigned retreat. Captured Rus' princes were crushed to death under a victory platform. The Mongols did not besiege major cities such as Kyiv until decades later.

The Mongol commanders Jebe and Subutai raided through the Caucasus after the fall of the Khwarezmian Empire, defeating the Cumans. The Cuman Khan fled to his son-in-law Mstislav the Bold, who formed an alliance of Rus' princes. The Mongols routed that alliance's army at the Kalka River on 31 May 1223.

On 3 September 1260, the Bahri Mamluks of Egypt defeated the Mongol Ilkhanate at Ain Jalut, marking the first major halt to Mongol advances. Hulegu had left about 10,000 troops under Kitbuqa after returning to Mongolia for a kurultai. The Mamluks used hit-and-run tactics, a feigned retreat by Baibars and a flanking maneuver by Qutuz, and a final counterattack killed many Mongols, including Kitbuqa himself. In retaliation for his death, a later Mongol force massacred a large number of Muslims at Aleppo in December 1260.

King Béla IV had personally supervised dense natural barriers along Hungary's eastern border to slow the Mongols. Mongol specialist units cleared the paths in just three days. Combined with a speed of advance a European observer called "lightning", this left the Hungarians no time to gather their forces.

Before the Battle of Mohi on 11 April 1241, the cautious Hungarian king ordered a heavily fortified camp of wagons, a battle-tested countermeasure against nomadic armies. It became a trap: the Mongols bombarded it with stones and flaming arrows, and terrified soldiers were trampled to death in the crush of their comrades. When the demoralized Hungarians fled through a gap the Mongols had left open on purpose, almost all of them were slaughtered, among them Archbishop Ugrin, another archbishop and three bishops. A near-contemporary source reports 10,000 Hungarians killed, and Thomas of Spalato wrote that the escape route was strewn with so many corpses that the ground was dyed red with blood. The Mongols themselves took heavy losses, which contributed to the decision to halt their campaign.

Two days before Mohi, on 9 April 1241, a combined force of Poles and Moravians under Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia fought the Mongols at Legnica. Mongol commanders Baidar and Kadan had heard that King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia was approaching with an army over twice the size of Henry's. They turned to intercept Henry before the European armies could join.

During the siege of Xiangyang, which lasted from 1268 to 1273, the Mongols set up a full naval blockade in 1271 that isolated the city. A Song relief convoy of a hundred paddle-wheel boats tried to run the blockade, but the Mongol fleet spread across the whole Yangtze and stretched a chain over the water. The Song forces suffered heavy casualties trying to cut through the chains with axes, pull up stakes and hurl bombs, and in 1273 the Mongols enlisted two Muslim engineers, one from Persia and one from Syria, who helped build counterweight trebuchets. These new siege weapons led to the surrender of Xiangyang.

Contemporary European accounts claimed more than 100,000 Mongols fought at Legnica. Historians call this a gross overestimate, since current estimates put the Mongol force at 25,000 cavalry at most. The Ystoria Mongalorum places the Mongol force that invaded Poland at 10,000 horsemen.

literature.text: Central Asia has an improvisational oral poetry tradition that is over 1000 years old. It is practiced mainly in Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan by akyns, who face each other in lyrical battles called the aytysh or the alym sabak. The tradition arose out of early bardic oral historians.

The Uyghur poet Ali-Shir Nava'i (1441–1501) offered strong arguments that the Turkic languages deserved poetic status, in contrast to the much-venerated Persian. Partly as a result of such arguments, Divan poetry came to show a unique balance of Persian and Turkish elements.

Rumi, one of the best-loved Persian poets, was born in Balkh (in modern Afghanistan) or Wakhsh (in modern Tajikistan). He wrote in Persian and lived in Konya, then the capital of the Seljuks in Anatolia.

The Ghaznavids conquered large territories in Central and South Asia and adopted Persian as their court language. This helped spread Persian literature well beyond Iran, including into other parts of Central Asia.

The chronicler Ibn Al-Athir wrote that Mongol invaders massacred and killed about 700,000 people in Merv. Hamdallah Mustawfi, who completed Tarikh-i Guzida in 1330, likewise wrote that Merv was still in ruins in the middle of the 14th century. One historian concedes that much of what such chroniclers produced were exaggerated estimates, yet still counts the population of Persia as falling from 2,500,000 to 250,000 through mass extermination and famine.
Akyns perform with a stringed instrument. In Kyrgyzstan this is a three-stringed komuz, and in Kazakhstan a similar two-stringed instrument called the dombra.

The name Khamag Mongol appears in only two passages of the Secret History of the Mongols and is absent from other known sources. Mongolist B. R. Zoriktuev, of Buryat origin, used this to question whether Khamag Mongol was ever an independent political entity in the early 12th century.

Under the Mongol rulers of the Ilkhanate, the Persian scholar Rashid-al-Din Hamadani began writing the Jami al-Tawarikh in 1300 at the order of Ilkhan Ghazan. It was completed in 1311 under Öljeitü and drew on the Altan Debter by the Mongol historian Bolad Chinsan.

science.text: Genghis Khan was proclaimed ruler of all Mongols in 1206, and his empire grew into the largest contiguous empire in history. Mongol armies used terror as a weapon: the population of a captured city, aside from useful people such as craftsmen, was usually massacred, and the Mongols spread news of these killings to frighten others into surrendering. Out of this conquest came an enforced Pax Mongolica, which allowed the exchange of trade, technologies, commodities, and ideologies across Eurasia.

In 1273 the Mongols enlisted the expertise of two Muslim engineers, one from Persia and one from Syria. They helped build counterweight trebuchets, and these new siege weapons resulted in the surrender of Xiangyang in 1273.

Important changes to the world economy in the 14th and 15th centuries reflected the development of nautical technology. Europeans pioneered ocean trade routes, and long-distance trade linking East Asia and India to Western Europe increasingly moved over the seas rather than through Central Asia.

The siege of Xiangyang and Fancheng lasted from 1268 to 1273. In 1271 the Mongols set up a full naval blockade, isolating the two cities. A Song relief convoy of a hundred paddle-wheel boats, led by Zhang Shun and Zhang Gui, ran the blockade and fought the Mongol fleet with fire-lances, fire-bombs and crossbows. The Song forces suffered heavy casualties as they tried to cut through the chains with axes, pull up stakes and hurl bombs.

At the siege of Shaoyang in 1274, the Mongol general Bayan waited for the wind to change to a northerly course. He then ordered his artillerists to bombard the city with molten metal bombs, which caused such a fire that "the buildings were burned up and the smoke and flames rose up to heaven." Shaoyang was captured and its inhabitants massacred.

After the Yuan dynasty fell in 1368, the Mongols continued to rule the Northern Yuan on the Mongolian steppe. The earliest written references to the plough in Middle Mongol language sources appear towards the end of the 14th century.
Bayan used bombs again in 1275 during the siege of Changzhou. He then stormed the walls and massacred the inhabitants because they had refused to surrender.

Shortly after the Mongol invasions of Japan in the late 13th century, the Japanese produced a scroll painting depicting a bomb called tetsuhau. It is speculated to have been the Chinese thunder crash bomb. Japanese descriptions also talk of iron and bamboo pao causing "light and fire" and emitting 2–3,000 iron bullets.

politics.text: In 1206 a council proclaimed Temüjin, known as Genghis Khan, ruler of all Mongols after he united several nomadic tribes. Along the way he had eradicated the Tatars in 1202 and Jamukha was executed. His empire then grew into the largest contiguous empire in history, stretching from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe. The Mongols' invading armies usually massacred the population of captured cities, aside from craftsmen and other useful people.

After Möngke Khan died in 1259 during the siege of Diaoyu Castle with no declared successor, the Tolui family line fought over the title of khagan in the Toluid Civil War. Ariq Böke captured and then executed Abishka, the Chagatai prince loyal to Kublai, and Kublai blockaded Ariq Böke in Mongolia to cut off his food supplies, causing a famine. This war helped split the empire into four khanates: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty.

Timur, a warlord of the Turco-Mongol Barlas tribe, founded the Timurid Empire in 1370 and ruled it until his death in 1405. He saw himself as the great restorer of the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan and regarded himself as his heir.

The Ilkhanate fell apart after its last ilkhan, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, died in 1335. In the 1330s the Black Death ravaged the realm, and both Abu Sa'id and his sons were dead of plague by 1335, leaving a string of short-lived khans.

The Timurids called themselves Gurkani, a Persianized form of the Mongolian word kürgen, meaning son-in-law. The title reflected that Timur had married Saray Mulk Khanum, a direct descendant of Genghis Khan, making the dynasty in-laws of his line.

Genghis Khan rose to power on the steppe through a string of victories and killings. Yesugei, his father, was poisoned by Tatars when Temüjin was still young, and Temüjin killed his older half-brother to secure his family position. In 1202 he eradicated the Tatars, and by about 1205 the Naimans were subjugated and his rival Jamukha was executed, leaving Temüjin the undisputed ruler of a newly unified people.

After Timur's death in 1405, Shahrukh Mirza emerged victorious from the first civil war and ruled from Herat. His son Ulugh Beg, based in Samarkand, was a famed patron of science and an astronomer himself, but was executed in 1449 after a revolt by his own son Abdal-Latif Mirza, plunging the empire into civil war.

Ilkhanid rulers began converting to Islam with Ghazan in 1295. In 1319 the Ilkhanid custodian Chupan crushed the rebel Anatolian emir Irenchin at the Battle of Zanjan-Rud. Chupan's influence also led the Ilkhanate to make peace with the Chagatais and the Mamluks.
In the 1330s, outbreaks of the Black Death ravaged the Ilkhanate. The last ilkhan, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, and his sons were killed by the plague by 1335, after which the Ilkhanate disintegrated.

In 1323 Abu Said Khan of the Ilkhanate signed a peace treaty with Egypt. At his request the Yuan court awarded his custodian Chupan the title of commander-in-chief of all Mongol khanates, but Chupan died in late 1327.

philosophy.text: Across the 13th and 14th centuries, the ruling Mongol elites of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Khanate gradually adopted Islam and Turkic languages. They still kept Mongol political and legal institutions. The result was an ethnocultural blend known as the Turco-Mongol tradition.

The Mongol Empire connected the East with the West in an enforced Pax Mongolica. That peace rested on terror: the Mongols usually massacred the population of captured cities, aside from craftsmen and other useful people, and encouraged news of it to spread so that others would surrender before a costly siege. Once the conquest was done, trade, technologies, commodities and ideologies were exchanged across Eurasia, from the Pacific to the Mediterranean.

The Timurid Empire had a syncretic culture that combined Turkic, Mongolic and Persian influences. Its last members were regarded as "ideal Perso-Islamic rulers". Timur founded it in 1370 and ruled until 1405.

Uzbeg took the throne of the Golden Horde in 1313 and made Islam the state religion. He proscribed Buddhism and Shamanism among the Mongols in Russia, reversing the spread of Yuan culture. By 1315 he had Islamicized the Horde by killing the Jochid princes and Buddhist lamas who opposed his religious policy and his succession to the throne.
Later Ilkhanid rulers, beginning with Ghazan in 1295, converted to Islam. The Ilkhanate was a Mongol khanate founded by Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan. It was known as the Land of Iran.

In 1256 the Nizari Ismaili Imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah surrendered to Hülegü while besieged at Maymun-Diz, after Mongol mangonels bombarded the fortress and hurled javelins dipped in burning pitch. A small part of the garrison refused to surrender and made a last stand in a high domed building; they were defeated and slaughtered after three days. Khurshah ordered his followers to capitulate, and Alamut was dismantled. The Nizari state was disestablished, though some forts kept resisting, and Möngke Khan later ordered a general massacre of all Nizaris, including Khurshah and his family.

Under Uzbeg and his successor Jani Beg (1342–1357), Islam gained general acceptance in the Golden Horde. Its adherents nonetheless remained tolerant of other beliefs. Among some Turks in Eurasia, Islam already had deep roots going back to pre-Mongol times.

Although the Ilkhanid rulers were of non-Iranian origin, they tried to advertise their authority by tying themselves to the Iranian past. Their realm was officially called the Land of Iran, or simply Iran.

After the Nizari state was disestablished, the Nizaris either were killed or abandoned their strongholds. Around 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed in Möngke's general massacre, and Ötegü-China summoned the Nizaris of Quhistan to gatherings and slaughtered about 12,000 of them. Many survivors were absorbed into Ismaili communities in Western, Central and South Asia, or assimilated into the local Sunni population while practicing taqiyya. Little is known about them afterward.

In 1275 a Nizari force under a son of Khurshah recaptured Alamut Castle, but the Mongols reclaimed it a year later. This came after Khurshah and his small retinue had been executed by their Mongol escort on the way home from Mongolia, and after the Mongols killed the surviving garrison of Gerdkuh in 1270. The Nizaris later re-established their Imamate at the village of Anjudan, where they are recorded as active in the 14th and 15th centuries.

culture.text: During the 13th and 14th centuries the Mongol elites of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Khanate assimilated into the Turkic populations they ruled. They gradually adopted Islam and Turkic languages, yet kept Mongol political and legal institutions. They became known as Turco-Mongols.
The Timurid Empire led to the Timurid Renaissance, particularly during the reign of Shahrukh Mirza (1405–1447). His son Ulugh Begh, who ruled 1447–1449, was an astronomer and mathematician.
Timur kept strong trade relations with Ming China and the Golden Horde. Chinese diplomats such as Ma Huan and Chen Cheng travelled west to his capital, Samarkand.

Ulugh Beg was based in Samarkand and was a famed patron of science, being an astronomer and mathematician himself. His execution in 1449, after a revolt by his son Abdal-Latif Mirza, plunged the empire into civil war.
